meta.blurb: Mira has two days to answer a job offer in another city, and her heart says yes. Follow her as she slows down, tests her feelings and learns how the mind can be fooled, so that she can make a calm choice she will not regret.
meta.bible: Mira: a young professional in her late twenties who receives a job offer in a distant city; excited, thoughtful and a little anxious. Lena: Mira's friend who tells a sad story about a move that went badly. Kofi: Mira's older colleague, who once moved cities for work; honest and kind. The story follows one decision over about a year: the offer, two days to answer, the weekend visit, the choice to say yes with a start date one month later, the first hard weeks and the review after six months. Ideas taught, in order: the quick way and the slow way of thinking; experts can be fast where practice and feedback exist; feeling sure is not evidence; vivid stories versus numbers; the outside view; loss feels bigger than gain; wording changes feelings; sunk costs; overconfidence; plans run late; imagine failure and success; mood and sleep; weighing what matters; asking others; small tests; reversible and permanent choices; rules and deadlines; writing reasons down; judging process and not only outcome; hindsight. Facts are general and hedged: no invented studies, numbers or quotes. Voice and tone: calm, clear, kind and practical, with plain examples.

B1B2: Mira opens an email that offers her a new job in a city far away. She has only two days to answer, and her heart is beating fast.
Your mind has two ways of working. One is quick and automatic, and the other is slow and careful, and good decisions need both.
The quick way of thinking is a wonderful tool. It lets you catch a ball, recognise a friend in a crowd and step back from a car, all without stopping to think.
The slow way of thinking is used for hard sums, careful plans and complicated choices. It takes effort, and you can often feel it, because it makes you slow and serious.
Slow thinking uses a lot of energy and attention, so it is tiring. Because of this, many people are tempted to trust their first feeling and skip the careful work.
After years of practice in a familiar field, an expert can often judge a situation very quickly and correctly. A chess master, for example, can look at a board and see the right idea at once.
Look at two lines of exactly the same length, one with arrows pointing inwards and one with arrows pointing outwards. They look different, and they still look different after you have measured them.
The illusion teaches a simple lesson. A strong feeling of certainty is not evidence, and it tells you how you feel but not whether you are right.
The slow way of thinking is often lazy, and it tends to agree with the quick way without checking it. That is why a real check needs a plan and not just good intentions.
Mira's first reaction to the offer is a big yes. The city looks exciting in the photographs, the salary is generous, and she is already imagining her new life.
Mira decides to slow down, and she writes the question at the top of a clean sheet of paper. A question that is written down is much easier to think about than a feeling in the chest.
Mira had thought that the choice was between yes and no. When she looks at the page, she sees other options, such as asking for more time or asking for a later start.
Mira's friend Lena tells her a sad story about a move that went badly. Mira cannot stop thinking about it, even though it is only one story out of many.

Things that are easy to remember seem more likely than they really are. Plane crashes make big news, for example, yet travelling by car is generally far more dangerous for every kilometre that you travel.
Mira decides to look for numbers as well as stories. She wonders how many people move for a job and are happy about it later, and she searches for any honest information.
Sometimes no exact numbers exist, and then a rough estimate is still better than nothing. Mira asks herself what usually happens in cases like hers, and she writes down a careful guess.
There are two ways to look at a plan. From the inside, Mira sees her own story, but from the outside, she can ask how similar plans usually turn out for other people.
For most people, losing something feels worse than gaining the same thing feels good. Mira worries much more about leaving her flat and friends than she enjoys thinking about her new salary.
To test the pull of a fear, you can turn the question around. Mira asks herself what she would do if she already lived in the new city and was offered her old life back.
The same facts can feel different when they are described in different words. A medicine that works for ninety out of a hundred people sounds better than one that fails for ten out of a hundred.
Mira writes her choice in two ways: what she might gain by moving, and what she might lose by staying. If her answer changes with the words, she knows that the words are pushing her.

Two years ago, Mira began a course that she no longer enjoys, and she feels that she must finish it because of the time and money already spent. Those costs are gone, and they should not decide her future.
Most people are more confident in their own judgement than the facts allow. It is wise to ask, how could I be wrong, and to write down at least three answers.
Plans usually take longer and cost more than we expect, and this happens to almost everyone. Mira thinks about her last three projects, and each of them took longer than she had planned.
So Mira adds a safety margin to her plan. She allows extra time for the move and some extra money for surprises, and she feels calmer as soon as she has done it.
Here is a useful trick. Mira imagines that it is one year in the future and that the move has gone badly, and then she asks herself what the most likely reasons are.
Next, she imagines that the move has been a great success, and she asks what made it work. She sees friends who visit, a good routine and a flat in a quiet street.
Mood has a strong effect on choices, and Mira knows it. She decides not to make her decision when she is hungry, tired or angry, and she waits for a calm moment.
When a strong feeling is pushing you, try to name it. Mira says to herself, I feel nervous, and she notices that the feeling becomes a little smaller once she has put a word on it.

Many people find that a night of sleep helps with a big decision, and some evidence suggests that rest does help the mind to sort out its thoughts. Mira goes to bed, and in the morning she feels clearer.
Before she compares the options, Mira lists what matters most to her. She writes four things: money, people, growth and home, and each of them is a different kind of value.
Next, Mira gives each item a number from one to five to show how important it is. Growth and people receive the highest numbers, and money gets a three.
Then she gives each option a score for each item on the list. The totals are interesting, but she knows that numbers are only a guide, and they cannot replace her own judgement.
Suppose the result feels wrong. Mira's list slightly favours staying, but she feels a strong pull towards the new city, and she decides to ask herself why.
When the list and the gut disagree, there is something to learn. Perhaps the list forgot something important, or perhaps the gut is simply afraid of change.
Mira asks her older colleague, Kofi, for a talk. He has no interest in what she chooses, and she knows that he will tell her the truth, even if it is not what she hopes to hear.
Mira asks Kofi to argue against the move on purpose. She does not want him to be cruel, but she wants to hear the best reasons against her plan so that she can test it.
Kofi himself once moved to a new city for work. Mira asks him what he would do differently, and his answer, which is to find friends quickly, is one that she writes down.
Be careful how you ask. If Mira says, You think I should go, don't you, most people will say yes to be kind, so she asks a more open question instead.
Instead of guessing, Mira decides to try a small test. She spends a weekend in the new city, and she sees the streets, the offices and the flats with her own eyes.
Some decisions can be changed later, and some cannot. Mira's job offer is hard to undo, so it deserves a lot of thought, but a choice of coffee does not.
For the small choices, Mira sets up simple rules, such as always eating the same breakfast. She saves her careful thinking for the decisions that really matter.

There is always more information to find, so Mira sets a deadline for herself. When the time comes, she stops searching, because a good decision that is made today is better than a perfect one that never arrives.
Before she chooses, Mira writes in a notebook. She records her reasons, what she expects to happen, and how sure she feels, and she dates the page so she can read it again later.
Mira has now thought about the choice slowly and carefully, and she decides to say yes. She asks for a start date one month later, and the company agrees.
A good decision can still bring a bad result, because the world contains chance. Mira's first weeks are hard and lonely, but that does not prove that her choice was wrong.
When the weeks are hard, Mira opens her notebook and reads her old reasons. She also reads Kofi's advice about making friends quickly, and she joins a walking club.
After six months, Mira reads her notes again. She is surprised by how much she had forgotten, and she is reminded that hindsight makes everything seem more obvious than it was.
By the end of the year, Mira feels at home in her new city. She knows that luck helped her, but she is glad that she did not rely only on a lucky feeling.
Here is the whole idea in a few lines. When a decision matters, slow down, check your first feeling, look for facts, ask someone honest, write it down, and then choose and move on.
C1C2: Mira opened an email at her desk and read that a company in a distant city wanted to hire her. The offer was generous, the deadline was two days away, and her heart was racing as though she had run up a flight of stairs. Somewhere in the next forty-eight hours she would have to make a choice that might shape the next several years of her life.

Your mind works in two quite different ways. The first is quick, automatic and effortless, while the second is slow, deliberate and rather hard work, and sound decisions usually need both of them. The trick is not to choose one over the other but to know which of them is in charge at any given moment.

The quick mind is a marvellous servant. It lets you catch a ball, recognise a friend's face across a crowded square and leap back from a speeding car, all before you have had time to form a single deliberate thought. Life would be impossible if every small judgement required slow, careful effort.

The slow way of thinking comes into play when you work out a complicated sum, compare two plans or fill in a tricky form. It demands effort, and you can feel that effort as a kind of tightening of the mind, a narrowing of the attention. Most of us find it uncomfortable and are tempted to avoid it whenever we can.

Slow thinking consumes attention, and attention is a limited resource that runs low after a long day. It is therefore tempting to accept whatever answer our first feeling offers and to avoid the tiring work of checking it. This is not a sign of weakness but a normal feature of the human mind, and knowing it is the first step towards managing it.

Experts in a familiar field can often judge a situation at a glance, because years of practice have taught the quick mind what to notice. A strong chess player looks at a board and sees a good idea almost at once, much as you see a word on a page without spelling it out. This kind of skill, however, develops only where situations repeat and the person receives honest feedback.

There is a famous drawing of two lines of exactly equal length, one finished with arrowheads that point inwards and the other with arrowheads that point outwards. They look quite different, and they go on looking different even after you have measured them with a ruler. The quick mind produced an answer, and knowing better does not always switch it off.

The illusion carries a useful lesson: a strong feeling of certainty is not the same thing as evidence. Certainty is a sensation, and it tells you how the mind feels about an answer but nothing about whether the answer is correct. Learning to doubt that sensation, politely and at the right moments, is one of the great skills of decision making.

The slow mind is often rather lazy, and instead of checking the quick mind's answers it frequently just nods and agrees with them. A real check therefore needs a plan and a few deliberate steps, because good intentions alone are rarely enough. This book will build such a plan, one small tool at a time, around a single real choice.

Mira's first reaction was an enormous yes. The city glittered in the photographs, the salary was generous, and she was already imagining herself in a bright new flat, walking to work along a river. She noticed, with a small flicker of suspicion, that her mind had made the whole decision before she had asked it a single question.

Mira decided to slow down, and she began by writing her question at the top of a clean sheet of paper. A question set out in plain words is far easier to examine than a feeling in the chest, and the act of writing forces the slow mind to wake up. The page, she found, was a patient listener.

Mira had assumed that her choice was simply between yes and no, but the page showed her that other options existed. She could ask for more time, request a later start date, or even negotiate a trial period before moving. Many hard decisions feel like a trap only because we have looked at too few ways out.

Mira's friend Lena told her a painful story about a move that had ended badly, and the story stayed in Mira's mind all evening. A vivid example has a strange power: it feels more important than it should, simply because it is easy to picture. One story is only one case, however sad it is.

Events that are easy to remember seem more common than they really are. Aeroplane accidents fill the news for days, for instance, yet travelling by car is generally far more dangerous for every kilometre that you cover. The ease with which an example comes to mind tells you about the drama of the story and not about the odds.

Mira decided to look for numbers as well as stories, and she asked herself a plain question: of all the people who move for a new job, how many are glad afterwards? She searched for honest surveys and statistics, aware that they could not predict her own future. Even a rough figure is a useful counterweight to a single vivid memory.

Sometimes the exact figures do not exist, and a careful guess is still better than a mere impression. Mira asked herself what usually happens in cases like hers and wrote down an honest estimate, however rough it was. The aim was not precision but a more sober starting point than her own excitement.

We can look at a plan from the inside, where we see only our own hopeful story, or from the outside, where we ask how similar plans usually turn out for other people. Mira tried to climb out of her own head and look down on her situation from a distance. The view was less glamorous than the one from inside, but it was a good deal more reliable.

For most people, a loss hurts more than an equal gain pleases, so we tend to guard what we have more fiercely than we pursue what we might win. Mira noticed that she was dwelling far more on leaving her flat and her friends than on the pleasure of her new salary. The pain of giving up something was louder than the joy of gaining something else.

A good way to test the pull of a fear is to turn the question around. Mira asked herself what she would do if she already lived in the new city and were offered her present life back as a prize. She found that she would not take it, and that told her something no list had been able to.

The very same facts can feel quite different when they are described in different words. A treatment that works for ninety people in a hundred sounds more attractive than one that fails for ten in a hundred, although the two descriptions say exactly the same thing. Researchers have shown this effect again and again, and it affects clever people as much as anyone.

Mira tried writing her choice in two different ways: what she might gain by moving, and what she might lose by staying. If her answer changed according to the words, she reasoned, then the words were doing the deciding and not she. A decision that survives both versions is sturdier than one that depends on the phrasing.

Two years ago Mira began a course that she no longer enjoyed, and she kept going because she had already spent so much time and money on it. Economists call such past costs sunk, meaning that they are gone whatever she chooses next. The only sensible question is what the remaining time and money will buy, and not what the earlier ones did.

Most of us are more confident in our own judgement than the evidence warrants, and the more we know about a subject, the easier it is to forget how much we do not know. A helpful habit is to ask, how could I be wrong, and to write down at least three honest answers. If you cannot think of any, that is itself a warning.

Most plans take longer and cost more than their authors expect, and almost everyone falls into this trap, even when they know about it. Mira thought about her last three projects and admitted that every one of them had run over time, however carefully she had planned. Optimism about our own future is a stubborn habit of the human mind.

Mira therefore built a safety margin into her plan, with extra time for the move and a little extra money for the surprises that always arrive. She felt calmer as soon as she had done so, because the plan no longer depended on everything going perfectly. A plan that survives a few mishaps is worth much more than one that works only in the best case.

Here is a surprisingly powerful trick: imagine that it is a year in the future and that your plan has failed completely, and then ask yourself why. Mira let herself picture the failure and found that reasons poured onto the page at once: loneliness, a difficult manager, a flat that was too expensive. Naming the dangers in advance made them far easier to prepare for.

Next she pictured the opposite outcome, in which the move had been a triumph, and asked what had made it so. The answers were encouraging and concrete: a quiet street, a regular routine, friends who came to visit and a manager who gave her room to grow. She realised that she could start building those conditions now.

Our mood and our body colour our decisions more than we like to admit, and Mira knew it. After an exhausting day and a missed lunch she found herself ready to reject the offer out of sheer irritation, so she promised herself not to decide in such a state. Calm is not a luxury in decision making but a working condition.

When a strong feeling is steering you, it helps to give it a name. Mira said quietly to herself, I feel nervous, and she noticed that the feeling shrank a little as soon as it had a word attached to it. Naming an emotion does not remove it, but it lets you treat it as information instead of an order.

Many people find that a night's sleep helps with a hard choice, and there is some evidence that rest helps the mind to organise what it has learned during the day. Mira went to bed with the question unresolved, and she woke the next morning feeling lighter and more orderly in her thinking. It is not magic, but it is free.

Before comparing the options, Mira listed what mattered most to her, and four words filled the page: money, people, growth and home. Each of them stood for a different kind of value, and none of them could be measured in the same units as the others. Putting them in words first protected her from letting the loudest one win.

Next Mira gave each item a weight from one to five according to how much it mattered to her. People and growth earned fives, home earned a four, and money, which she had thought would matter most, received only a three. The weights surprised her, and the surprise was a small but valuable discovery.

Then she scored each option against each item on the list and added up the totals. The numbers were interesting, but she treated them as a guide and not as a verdict, because a score is only as honest as the person who writes it. Their real value was that they made her thinking visible, so that she could examine it.

Suppose the answer on the page feels wrong. Mira's list slightly favoured staying where she was, yet she felt a strong pull in the other direction, and she decided to treat that pull as a question and not as an error. Feelings are sometimes a form of knowledge that has not yet found its words.

When the list and the gut disagree, the disagreement is a clue. Perhaps the list has forgotten something that matters, or perhaps the gut is simply frightened of change, and the task is to find out which of the two is speaking. Mira discovered that her list had left out adventure, which mattered to her a great deal.

Mira asked for a talk with her older colleague Kofi, who had nothing to gain from her choice and who was known for telling the truth kindly. Over coffee she explained everything, and she was struck by how different her own story sounded when she had to say it out loud to another person. A good listener is a mirror that talks back.

Mira asked Kofi to argue against the move, as strongly as he honestly could, and he agreed with a smile. She wanted not a quarrel but a test, because a plan that has never faced an objection has never really been examined. Several of his points were new to her, and one of them changed her plans.

Kofi himself had once moved to a new city for work, and Mira asked what he would do differently if he were to do it again. His answer was to build friendships far earlier, and not to wait until the loneliness arrived, and she wrote it down at once. Questions about the past are often more useful than questions about the future, because the past has already happened.

Be careful how you ask for advice, since people tend to give the answer they think you want. If Mira had said, you think I should go, don't you, almost anyone would have nodded to be kind, so she asked an open question instead and kept her own opinion out of it. The quality of the advice depends heavily on the quality of the question.

Rather than guessing, Mira decided to run a small, cheap test, and she spent a weekend in the new city. She walked from the station to the office, looked at three flats and ate her dinner in an ordinary restaurant, as she would on a normal evening. An hour of real experience, she found, is worth more than a day of imagination.

Some choices can be undone with little cost, while others cannot be reversed at all, and the careful thinker spends effort accordingly. Mira's job offer was in the second group, since a move would cost money and friendships, whereas her choice of coffee in the cafe was in the first. Spending an hour on a small choice is a quiet waste of the slow mind.

For the small and repeated choices, Mira set up simple rules, such as eating the same breakfast and keeping a fixed time for answering email. This saved her slow mind for the decisions that really mattered, in the way that a sensible traveller packs light so as to keep her strength for the hills. A few good defaults make the rest of life lighter.

There is always more information that you could gather, and the search can become a way of avoiding the choice. Mira therefore set herself a deadline, and when it arrived she stopped looking, accepting that a good decision made today is worth more than a perfect one that never comes. Waiting for certainty is a decision too, and rarely a wise one.

Before she made her choice, Mira wrote everything in a notebook: her reasons, what she expected to happen, and how confident she felt, and she dated the page carefully. This record would later let her judge her thinking honestly, since memory has an unfortunate habit of rewriting itself to flatter us. A decision that has been written down cannot be quietly changed afterwards.

Having thought about the choice slowly and carefully, Mira decided to say yes, and what struck her was how calm she felt as she wrote the reply. She asked for a start date one month later so that she would have time to say goodbye properly, and the company agreed at once. The decision felt very different from the first rush of excitement, for it rested on something steadier.

A good decision can still lead to a poor result, because chance plays a part in everything, and a bad decision can sometimes be rescued by luck. Mira's first weeks in the new city were hard and lonely, but that did not prove that her thinking had been wrong. We should judge a choice by the quality of the process as well as by the outcome.

When the weeks felt hard, Mira opened her notebook and read what she had written before the move. She found Kofi's advice about making friends early, and the next day she joined a walking club and began, at last, to feel less alone. Her notes had become a patient friend that told her what she already knew.

Six months later Mira read her notes again and was surprised by how much she had forgotten, and by how different her expectations had been from what actually happened. This is the trick of hindsight: once we know how a story ends, it seems that we always knew. Honest records protect us from that comfortable illusion and let us learn from our real mistakes.

By the end of the year Mira felt entirely at home in her new city, with friends, a routine and work that stretched her. She knew that luck had played its part, as it always does, but she was glad that she had not relied on a lucky feeling alone. She had made the choice with her eyes open, and that was something she could repeat.

Here, then, is the whole idea in a few lines. When a decision truly matters, slow down and notice your first feeling, look for facts and numbers, imagine failure and success, ask an honest person to argue with you, and write down your reasons. Then choose, and let go of the choice, because a calm decision is not one that is certain but one that was made with care.
